spans.assertion: the hypothesis that referees are biased against dark-skinned players is not supported by the analysis

after adjusting for player position, league, physical characteristics, number of games, and referee country bias measures, dark-skinned players had an estimated 0.14 percentage point higher probability of receiving a red card (95% CI: -0.08 to 0.36, p=0.218)
this effect is not statistically significant and the confidence interval includes zero
all sensitivity analyses confirmed non-significant findings
the data provide no convincing evidence of red card bias based on player skin tone
the adjusted risk difference is 0.14 percentage points (95% CI: [-0.08, 0.36], p=0.218, two-sided)
the estimand is the adjusted absolute difference in red card probability between dark-skinned (>0.5) and light-skinned (≤0.25) players, controlling for confounders
dark-skinned players have an estimated 0.14 percentage point higher red card probability, not statistically distinguishable from zero, with CI from -0.08 to +0.36 pp
given the baseline red card rate of 1.2%, even the upper confidence limit (0.36 pp) would represent a modest effect
the adjusted odds ratio is 1.12 (95% CI: [0.93, 1.36], p=0.218)
the adjusted odds of a red card are 1.12 times higher for dark-skinned vs light-skinned players, with CI including the null value of 1.0, indicating no significant association
the unadjusted (crude) OR was 1.08 (95% CI: [0.94, 1.25])
the closeness of crude and adjusted ORs suggests minimal confounding
the unit of analysis is the player-referee dyad, i.e. one row per player paired with one referee across all games they encountered each other
the original dataset contained 146,028 dyads across 2,053 players and 3,147 referees
after excluding missing skin tone ratings, 124,621 dyads remained (1,586 players with photos)
the primary analysis sample restricted to dark vs light skin tone only was 110,023 dyads
the final modeling sample after complete-case restriction was 101,718 dyads (1,242 players, 2,775 referees)
light skin was defined as ≤0.25 on the 0-1 scale, comprising 83,582 dyads (82.2%)
dark skin was defined as >0.5 on the 0-1 scale, comprising 18,136 dyads (17.8%)
skin tone was rated by two independent coders on a 5-point scale and then averaged
inter-rater reliability was excellent (Pearson r=0.92, Spearman r=0.86)
middle skin tones (0.25-0.5) were excluded from the primary analysis to maximize contrast between exposure groups
the outcome was a binary indicator of whether the player received any red card(s) from that referee across all games in the dyad
overall red card prevalence was 1.23%
light-skinned players had a red card rate of 1.22%
dark-skinned players had a red card rate of 1.31%
the crude risk difference was 0.10 percentage points
player position (11 categories) was included as a covariate because positions differ in aggression/physicality and defenders receive more cards
league country (England, France, Germany, Spain) was included as a covariate because officiating styles vary by country
France had the highest red card rate (1.64%) and Germany the lowest (0.88%)
player height (continuous, standardized) was included as a covariate because taller/larger players may be perceived as more aggressive
player weight (continuous, standardized) was included as a covariate as a proxy for physical size
number of games in the dyad (continuous, standardized) was included as a covariate as an exposure adjustment since more games means more opportunities for red cards
referee country mean implicit bias (IAT score) was included as a covariate
referee country implicit bias was statistically significant (p=0.0005), indicating higher implicit bias associated with more red cards
referee country mean explicit bias (racial thermometer score) was included as a covariate
logistic regression was used as the modeling method
the outcome modeled was any red card (yes/no)
cluster-robust standard errors, clustered by player, were used to account for multiple dyads per player
the analysis was performed using Python statsmodels
21,407 dyads (14.7%) were excluded for missing skin tone ratings, i.e. players without photos or unavailable rater scores
players without photos were disproportionately from England/France and had fewer games
14,598 dyads (11.7%) with middle skin tones (0.25 to 0.5) were excluded to maximize contrast
8,305 dyads (7.5%) were excluded for missing confounders: position (7%), height (0.04%), weight (0.6%), or referee bias scores (0.1%)
continuous covariates (height, weight, games, implicit/explicit bias) were standardized to mean=0, SD=1
skin tone was averaged from two raters and dichotomized for the primary analysis
cluster-robust standard errors by player were used to account for within-player correlation
no survey weights were applied
clustering by player was used to accommodate within-player dependence
no fixed effects for player or referee were used; cluster-robust SEs were used instead
the overall conclusion is NOT SUPPORTED
the hypothesis that referees are more likely to give red cards to dark-skinned players is not supported by the data
the adjusted risk difference is very small (0.14 pp on a 1.2% baseline rate)
the 95% CI includes zero and spans a wide range (-0.08 to +0.36 pp)
the two-sided p-value is 0.218, above the α=0.05 threshold
the point estimate is positive (suggesting slightly more red cards for dark-skinned players) but is not distinguishable from chance variation

the study had 80% power to detect effects of 0.25 pp or larger, and the observed effect (0.14 pp) was only 55% of the minimum detectable effect, indicating the study is underpowered for effects of this size
multiple sensitivity analyses (continuous skin tone, alternative cutoffs, restricted samples, models without position) all showed non-significant results
